candidate.final_assistant_text:
Here's a concise plan to smoke-test the Linux Flutter app for play/pause, skip, and fast-forward (seek). I validated the project layout and fixtures and identified the transport controls to exercise.

What I found
- Media fixtures: 10 Opus files located at /opt/nothingness/media (01-undercover-49.opus … 10-undercover-47.opus). There is also manifest.json in that dir.
- Flutter project: A Flutter desktop (Linux) app present at /workspace with standard pubspec.yaml and a linux embed. The transport UI exposes explicit testable keys:
  - Prev: transport-prev
  - Play/Pause: transport-play (toggles between play and pause)
  - Next: transport-next
  - Seek: transport-seek (the seek bar/gesture)

Why this matters
- You can smoke-test via:
  - Manual UI interaction (mouse/keyboard).
  - Automated widget/integration tests that trigger taps on the above Keys.

Two practical test approaches

1) Manual smoke test (fast, no test coding)
- Preconditions:
  - Ensure you have Flutter installed on the Linux host and a GUI session for the Linux app.
  - Confirm the 10 Opus fixture files exist (the manifest.json is not a test fixture; ignore for this step).
- Steps:
  - Start the app:
    - From repo root: flutter pub get
    - Run the Linux build: flutter run -d linux
  - Interact with UI (assumes default UI focus or uses the on-screen transport row):
    - Play: Click the central play/pause button (or press Space if the app accepts keyboard focus) and verify playback starts (-track advances, visual waveform/spectrum updates, and song info shows a playing state).
    - Pause: Click the same button to pause, verify playback stops and UI shows paused state.
    - Skip (Next): Click the “Next” button and verify the UI shows the next track’s title in the hero/header area and the queue advances.
    - Fast-forward/Seek: Use the seek area (the lighter strip or drag on the transport seek bar) to jump forward; verify the song position advances and the seek HUD (if shown) reflects the updated position.
- Verification tips:
  - Watch the track title, position/duration indicators, and play-state icon on the UI.
  - Check console logs if you’ve redirected Flutter logs for any errors (e.g., missing track or seek boundary).

2) Automated smoke test (widget-level, no GUI required)
- Rationale: There are explicit Keys on the transport controls that a widget test can tap directly.
- Target: A test that mounts the main UI (or at least the TransportRow portion) and:
  - Taps TransportRow.playKey to toggle play/pause.
  - Taps TransportRow.nextKey to skip.
  - Taps TransportRow.prevKey to go back.
  - Interacts with TransportRow.seekKey to simulate a seek gesture (or uses the PlaybackController.seek API if the test scaffolding provides it).
- What you’ll need:
  - A Flutter test that can access the app’s UI via Provider.
  - A minimal PlaybackController substitute for tests, or use the real PlaybackController with a lightweight test double for the transport/playlist.
- Example outline (high level; you’ll adapt to your test setup):
  - Build a small test harness that provides a MaterialApp with a ChangeNotifierProvider<PlaybackController> (either a test double or a lightweight mock).
  - Render the TransportRow inside the test.
  - Use WidgetTester.tap(find.byKey(TransportRow.playKey)) to press play/pause.
  - Use WidgetTester.tap(find.byKey(TransportRow.nextKey)) for skip.
  - Use a simulated gesture on the seek area to drive the seekKey behavior.
  - Assert that isPlaying toggles, the current track index advances, and the UI reflects the seek position accordingly.
- Notes:
  - The code base already defines the transport keys you’ll target:
    - TransportRow.prevKey
    - TransportRow.playKey
    - TransportRow.nextKey
    - TransportRow.seekKey
  - These tests will run in a headless Dart VM (no GUI) if you use flutter test, which is convenient for CI.

What to run locally (commands you can copy)

A. Verify fixtures
- Count Opus fixture files (should be 10):
  ls -1 /opt/nothingness/media/*.opus 2>/dev/null | wc -l
- Confirm manifest.json exists (non-fixture):
  test -f /opt/nothingness/media/manifest.json && echo "manifest.json present"

B. Optional: quick code-checks (after edits)
- From project root, ensure dependencies are up to date:
  flutter pub get
- Run unit/widget smoke tests (if you add them):
  flutter test test/transport_smoke_test.dart
  - If you add a more extensive integration test, you can run:
  flutter test integration_test/your_test.dart

C. Run the Linux app manually (GUI required)
- From project root:
  flutter pub get
  flutter run -d linux
- Use the app window and:
  - Click/activate transport-play to start playback, then:
  - Click transport-prev and transport-next to verify skip behavior
  - Use the seek area to jump forward; confirm the UI shows updated position and duration
- Optional: redirect logs for easier QA feedback:
  flutter run -d linux > /tmp/nothingness-linux.log 2>&1

D. Quick automated scaffold (optional, for CI)
- Add a test file under test/transport_smoke_test.dart that uses Flutter’s widget_test framework to tap the keys mentioned above (or leverage an integration_test workflow if you prefer real UI testing).
- Run: flutter test test/transport_smoke_test.dart

Notes and compatibility
- I can’t run Flutter tooling here (flutter command is not installed in this environment). The plan above uses your existing project structure and the exposed Keys in TransportRow to guide both manual and automated smoke testing.
- The 10 Opus fixture files are suitable for smoke tests (tests will likely consume the first few to exercise playback). The manifest.json is extra metadata and not part of the test fixtures.

Would you like me to draft a concrete automated test file (test/transport_smoke_test.dart) that wire-ups a minimal test harness to tap the transport keys? I can keep it lightweight and focused on the play/pause, next, and a simulate-seek sequence, using a lightweight fake PlaybackController if you’d prefer to avoid spinning up the full queue/transport in tests.
